items.name: Farming begins
facts: People in the Fertile Crescent (modern Iraq, Syria, Turkey and Israel) began growing wheat and barley.
They tamed sheep, goats, cattle and pigs.
Farming started separately in China, Mexico, the Andes and Africa.
It let people settle in one place, and populations grew.

items.name: First cities in Mesopotamia
facts: Uruk, in modern Iraq, was one of the first true cities, with tens of thousands of people.
Sumerian cities had temples, kings, trade and craftsmen.
Mesopotamia means the land between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates.

items.name: Writing invented
facts: Sumerians pressed marks into wet clay with a reed; this is called cuneiform.
It began as a way of keeping accounts of grain and animals.
Egyptian hieroglyphs appeared at about the same time.
Writing marks the start of recorded history.

items.name: Stonehenge
facts: The stone circle on Salisbury Plain was built in stages over about 1,000 years.
The big sarsen stones were raised around 2500 BC.
The smaller bluestones were brought from Wales, over 200 kilometres away.

items.name: Indus Valley civilisation
facts: Cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, in modern Pakistan, had grid streets and drains.
The people used standard weights and traded with Mesopotamia.
Their script has never been read.

items.name: Great Pyramid of Giza
facts: Built as a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu.
At about 146 metres it was the tallest building in the world for almost 4,000 years.
It is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world still standing.

items.name: Hammurabi's law code
facts: Hammurabi, king of Babylon, had nearly 300 laws carved on a tall stone.
It is one of the oldest surviving law codes.
A famous rule: an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.
The stone is now in the Louvre in Paris.

items.name: Shang dynasty in China
facts: The first Chinese dynasty with written records.
Kings asked questions of their ancestors on oracle bones, giving the earliest Chinese writing.
The Shang were skilled makers of bronze vessels.
They were overthrown by the Zhou in 1046 BC.

items.name: Bronze Age collapse
facts: Many cities around the eastern Mediterranean were destroyed or abandoned.
The Hittite empire fell and Mycenaean Greece went into a dark age.
Causes may include drought, earthquakes, raiders known as the Sea Peoples and the collapse of trade.

items.name: The Olmecs
facts: The first major civilisation in Mexico and Central America.
They are famous for carving giant stone heads, some 3 metres tall.
Later peoples such as the Maya and Aztecs borrowed from Olmec culture.

items.name: Phoenician alphabet
facts: The Phoenicians, sea traders from modern Lebanon, used a simple alphabet of 22 letters.
The Greeks adopted it around 800 BC and added vowels.
Most alphabets used today, including ours, descend from it.

items.name: First Olympic Games
facts: Held at Olympia in Greece in honour of the god Zeus.
The first recorded event was a running race of about 190 metres.
Games were held every four years for over 1,000 years.

items.name: Rome founded
facts: According to legend, Rome was founded by Romulus, who killed his twin brother Remus.
Rome was ruled by kings until 509 BC, when it became a republic.
The real city grew from villages on hills by the river Tiber.

items.name: Kush rules Egypt
facts: Kings from Kush, in modern Sudan, conquered Egypt and ruled as its 25th dynasty.
Kush built more pyramids than Egypt, many at Meroe.
The Assyrians drove the Kushites out of Egypt around 660 BC.

items.name: Cyrus founds the Persian Empire
facts: Cyrus the Great united the Persians and Medes.
He conquered Babylon in 539 BC and let the exiled Jews return to Jerusalem.
His successors ruled the largest empire the world had seen, from Egypt to India.

items.name: Confucius
facts: A Chinese teacher whose ideas shaped China for 2,000 years.
He taught respect for elders, duty, good conduct and education.
His sayings were collected in the Analects.

items.name: The Buddha
facts: Siddhartha Gautama, a prince in what is now Nepal, gave up his wealth to seek the end of suffering.
He became the Buddha, the enlightened one, and taught a middle way between luxury and hardship.
Buddhism spread across Asia and has hundreds of millions of followers today.

items.name: Democracy in Athens
facts: Cleisthenes gave all male citizens of Athens a say in government.
Citizens voted in person in an assembly; women, slaves and foreigners were excluded.
The word democracy means rule by the people.

items.name: Persian Wars
facts: The Greeks defeated two Persian invasions.
The Athenians won at Marathon in 490 BC.
In 480 BC, 300 Spartans died at Thermopylae, and the Greek fleet won at Salamis.
Athens then had a golden age and built the Parthenon.

items.name: Alexander the Great
facts: King of Macedon at 20, he conquered the Persian Empire in about ten years.
His empire stretched from Greece to Egypt and the border of India.
He died in Babylon aged 32.
Greek culture spread across the Middle East in his wake.

items.name: Ashoka rules India
facts: Ashoka ruled the Mauryan Empire, which covered most of India.
After a bloody war in Kalinga he turned to Buddhism and non-violence.
He had his laws and ideas carved on pillars and rocks across India.
His lion capital is the emblem of modern India.

items.name: Qin unifies China
facts: Qin Shi Huang conquered the other warring states and became the first emperor of China.
He standardised writing, weights, coins and the width of cart axles.
He joined earlier walls to form the first Great Wall.
He was buried with the Terracotta Army of about 8,000 clay soldiers.

items.name: Han dynasty
facts: The Han ruled China for 400 years and gave the Chinese people their name.
Trade along the Silk Road linked China to Persia and Rome.
Paper-making was perfected in China around 105 AD.

items.name: Julius Caesar killed
facts: Caesar conquered Gaul (France) and made himself dictator of Rome.
He was stabbed to death by senators on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BC.
After civil war his heir Octavian became Augustus, the first emperor, in 27 BC.

items.name: Jesus of Nazareth
facts: Jesus was born in Judaea, a Roman province, probably a few years before 1 AD.
He taught for about three years and was crucified under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate.
His followers founded Christianity, now the world's largest religion.
Our calendar counts years from his birth.

items.name: Romans invade Britain
facts: The emperor Claudius sent four legions to conquer Britain.
Boudica led a revolt in 60 or 61 AD and burned London.
Hadrian's Wall was built from 122 AD to guard the northern frontier.
Roman rule lasted until about 410 AD.

items.name: Maya classic period
facts: Maya cities such as Tikal flourished in modern Guatemala, Mexico and Belize.
The Maya had a full writing system, accurate calendars and the idea of zero.
Most of the big cities were abandoned around 900.

items.name: Constantine and Christianity
facts: The emperor Constantine made Christianity legal in the Roman Empire.
He founded a new capital, Constantinople, in 330.
In 380 Christianity became the official religion of the empire.

items.name: Gupta Empire
facts: A golden age of India for art, maths and science.
Indian mathematicians developed the decimal number system we use today.
The astronomer Aryabhata worked out that the Earth spins.

items.name: Aksum adopts Christianity
facts: Aksum, in modern Ethiopia and Eritrea, was a rich trading kingdom.
King Ezana made it one of the first Christian states.
Ethiopia has been largely Christian ever since.

items.name: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
facts: Germanic tribes had been moving into the empire for a century.
Rome was sacked by the Visigoths in 410 and the Vandals in 455.
In 476 the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed.
The eastern empire, based in Constantinople, lasted another 1,000 years.

items.name: Tang dynasty
facts: China's Tang period was a golden age of poetry, art and trade.
Its capital Chang'an was probably the biggest city in the world.
Woodblock printing began in China in this period.

items.name: Muhammad and the birth of Islam
facts: Muhammad, a merchant from Mecca, taught that there is one God, Allah.
In 622 he moved to Medina; this move, the Hijra, starts the Muslim calendar.
By his death in 632 most of Arabia was Muslim.
Within a century Arab armies ruled from Spain to the borders of India.

items.name: Viking Age
facts: The first big Viking raid in England struck the monastery at Lindisfarne in 793.
Vikings from Scandinavia raided, traded and settled across Europe.
Alfred the Great stopped them conquering all of England in 878.
They reached Iceland, Greenland and, around 1000, North America.

items.name: Charlemagne crowned emperor
facts: Charlemagne, king of the Franks, united much of western Europe.
The Pope crowned him emperor in Rome on Christmas Day 800.
He supported learning and schools.
Both France and Germany claim him as a founder.

items.name: Song dynasty
facts: Song China developed paper money, the magnetic compass for navigation and gunpowder weapons.
Movable type printing was invented around 1040.
The Mongols conquered the Song in 1279.

items.name: Norman Conquest
facts: William, Duke of Normandy, defeated King Harold at the Battle of Hastings.
Harold had just marched south after beating a Viking army at Stamford Bridge.
The Normans built castles, and French words poured into English.
The Domesday Book of 1086 recorded who owned what.

items.name: First Crusade
facts: Pope Urban II called on Christians to take Jerusalem from Muslim rule.
The crusaders captured Jerusalem in 1099.
Saladin retook it in 1187, and crusades went on for two centuries.

items.name: Great Zimbabwe
facts: A stone city in southern Africa, home to perhaps 18,000 people.
Its rulers grew rich from cattle and the gold trade with the coast.
The name Zimbabwe comes from a Shona phrase meaning houses of stone.

items.name: Genghis Khan
facts: Temujin united the Mongol tribes and took the name Genghis Khan.
The Mongols built the largest land empire in history, from China to eastern Europe.
His grandson Kublai Khan ruled China.
The empire made trade along the Silk Road safer.

items.name: Magna Carta
facts: English barons forced King John to seal the Great Charter at Runnymede.
It said the king must obey the law and could not jail free men without lawful judgment.
It is seen as a foundation of the rule of law.

items.name: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage
facts: Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire in West Africa, went on pilgrimage to Mecca.
He gave away so much gold that its price in Cairo fell.
Timbuktu became a centre of Islamic learning.

items.name: Tenochtitlan founded
facts: The Aztecs built their capital on an island in a lake in central Mexico.
By 1500 it had around 200,000 people, larger than any city in Europe.
Mexico City now stands on the site.

items.name: Black Death
facts: Plague spread from Asia along trade routes to Europe.
It killed around a third to a half of Europe's people.
It was carried by fleas on rats and by human breath.
Labour became scarce, so wages rose for the survivors.

items.name: Zheng He's voyages
facts: The Ming emperor sent admiral Zheng He on seven huge voyages.
His fleets reached India, Arabia and East Africa.
His largest ships were far bigger than those of Columbus.
After 1433 China stopped the voyages.

items.name: Inca Empire expands
facts: Under Pachacuti the Incas spread out from Cusco in Peru.
The empire grew to run 4,000 kilometres along the Andes.
It had roads, bridges and stores, but no writing or wheels.
Machu Picchu was built around 1450.

items.name: Printing press
facts: Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz, Germany, printed with movable metal type.
His Bible of about 1455 was the first major printed book in Europe.
Books became cheap and ideas spread fast.
William Caxton set up the first press in England in 1476.

items.name: Fall of Constantinople
facts: The Ottoman Turks under Mehmed II captured the city after a 53-day siege.
This ended the eastern Roman, or Byzantine, Empire.
Constantinople, now Istanbul, became the Ottoman capital.

items.name: Columbus reaches the Americas
facts: Sailing for Spain, Columbus landed in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492.
He thought he had reached Asia.
Europe, Africa and the Americas were linked for the first time, exchanging crops, animals and deadly diseases.
In the same year Spain conquered Granada, the last Muslim state in Spain.

items.name: Vasco da Gama reaches India
facts: The Portuguese sailor found a sea route from Europe round Africa to India.
Portugal built a trading empire in the Indian Ocean.
Spices could now reach Europe without passing through Muslim lands.

items.name: The Reformation
facts: Martin Luther, a German monk, posted 95 theses attacking the sale of pardons by the Church.
He said people are saved by faith, and that the Bible, not the Pope, is the authority.
Western Christianity split into Catholic and Protestant.
Henry VIII broke with Rome in 1534 and made himself head of the Church of England.

items.name: Spanish conquest of the Aztecs
facts: Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico with about 500 men.
He allied with peoples who hated the Aztecs, and smallpox killed many defenders.
Tenochtitlan fell in 1521 and became Mexico City.

items.name: Mughal Empire founded
facts: Babur, descended from Timur and Genghis Khan, defeated the Sultan of Delhi at Panipat.
The Mughals ruled most of India for two centuries.
Akbar was tolerant of other faiths; Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal.

items.name: Spanish conquest of the Incas
facts: Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa with fewer than 200 men.
Atahualpa paid a room full of gold as ransom but was killed anyway.
Spain took over Peru and its silver mines.

items.name: Copernicus
facts: Copernicus published a book saying the Earth goes round the Sun.
Until then most people believed the Earth was the centre of the universe.
His idea started the Scientific Revolution.

items.name: Atlantic slave trade
facts: Over 350 years about 12.5 million Africans were shipped across the Atlantic.
Around 2 million died on the voyage.
They were forced to work on sugar, tobacco and cotton plantations.
Britain was a leading slave-trading nation in the 1700s.

items.name: Spanish Armada
facts: Philip II of Spain sent 130 ships to invade England.
English fireships and storms scattered the fleet.
Elizabeth I's England was confirmed as a Protestant power.

items.name: Tokugawa shogunate
facts: Tokugawa Ieyasu united Japan after a century of civil war.
The shoguns ruled from Edo, now Tokyo.
From the 1630s Japan shut itself off from most foreign contact for 200 years.

items.name: Galileo's telescope
facts: Galileo turned a telescope to the sky and saw moons orbiting Jupiter.
This showed that not everything circles the Earth.
The Church tried him in 1633 and kept him under house arrest for the rest of his life.

items.name: Thirty Years' War
facts: A war between Catholic and Protestant powers, fought mainly in Germany.
About a third of the people in some German lands died.
The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 set up the idea of independent sovereign states.

items.name: English Civil War
facts: Parliament fought King Charles I over power, money and religion.
Parliament won and Charles was beheaded in 1649.
Oliver Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector; the monarchy returned in 1660.

items.name: Newton's Principia
facts: Isaac Newton set out his laws of motion and gravity.
One set of laws explained both falling apples and the orbits of planets.
He also invented calculus and showed white light is made of colours.

items.name: Glorious Revolution
facts: Parliament invited William of Orange to replace the Catholic king James II.
James fled, and William and Mary took the throne.
The Bill of Rights of 1689 limited the power of the crown.

items.name: The Enlightenment
facts: Thinkers such as Locke, Voltaire, Rousseau and Kant argued for reason, science and liberty.
Ideas of rights and the consent of the governed inspired the American and French revolutions.
The French Encyclopédie tried to gather all knowledge in one work.

items.name: Seven Years' War
facts: A world war between Britain and France and their allies.
Britain won Canada and much of India; France lost most of its empire.
Its cost led Britain to tax the American colonies.

items.name: Industrial Revolution
facts: Britain was the first country to use machines and steam power on a large scale.
James Watt improved the steam engine in the 1770s.
People moved from farms to factory towns.
The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in 1830.

items.name: American independence
facts: Thirteen British colonies declared independence on 4 July 1776.
Britain recognised the United States in 1783 after losing the war.
The US Constitution of 1787 created a republic with an elected president.

items.name: French Revolution
facts: Crowds stormed the Bastille prison in Paris on 14 July 1789.
The revolution ended the monarchy; Louis XVI was guillotined in 1793.
Its ideals were liberty, equality and fraternity.
The Terror of 1793 to 1794 killed thousands.

items.name: Haitian Revolution
facts: Enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose up.
Led by Toussaint Louverture, they defeated French, British and Spanish forces.
Haiti became the first state founded by former slaves.

items.name: Napoleon and Waterloo
facts: Napoleon crowned himself Emperor of the French in 1804.
He conquered most of Europe but lost an army in Russia in 1812.
Wellington and Blücher defeated him at Waterloo in 1815.
He died in exile on St Helena in 1821.

items.name: Abolition of slavery in the British Empire
facts: Britain banned the slave trade in 1807 after a campaign led by Wilberforce and others.
Slavery itself was abolished across most of the empire in 1833.
France abolished slavery in 1848, the USA in 1865 and Brazil in 1888.

items.name: Latin American independence
facts: Spain's colonies broke away while Spain was weakened by Napoleon.
Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín led the armies.
Brazil left Portugal peacefully in 1822.

items.name: Opium Wars
facts: Britain fought China to keep selling opium there.
China lost and had to open ports and hand over Hong Kong.
A century of foreign pressure on China followed.

items.name: Revolutions of 1848
facts: Uprisings broke out in France, Germany, Italy, Austria and elsewhere.
People demanded constitutions, votes and national freedom.
Most were crushed within a year.
Marx and Engels published the Communist Manifesto the same year.

items.name: Indian Rebellion
facts: Indian soldiers in the East India Company's army rose up against British rule.
The revolt was put down with great bloodshed.
In 1858 the British Crown took direct control of India; this was the Raj.

items.name: Darwin's Origin of Species
facts: Charles Darwin explained how species evolve by natural selection.
His ideas came partly from his voyage on HMS Beagle.
The book changed how people saw life and humanity's place in nature.

items.name: US Civil War
facts: Eleven southern states left the Union to keep slavery.
About 620,000 soldiers died, more than in any other American war.
Lincoln's Union won; slavery was abolished by the 13th Amendment in 1865.
Lincoln was assassinated in April 1865.

items.name: Unification of Italy
facts: Garibaldi, Cavour and King Victor Emmanuel II joined the Italian states into one kingdom.
Rome became the capital in 1870.

items.name: Meiji Restoration
facts: Power was returned to the emperor and the shogunate ended.
Japan modernised fast, copying Western industry, schools and armies.
By 1905 Japan had defeated Russia in a war.

items.name: Unification of Germany
facts: Prussia's chancellor Otto von Bismarck united the German states through three wars.
The German Empire was declared at Versailles after defeating France.
A powerful new state changed the balance of Europe.

items.name: Scramble for Africa
facts: At the Berlin Conference, European powers agreed rules for carving up Africa.
By 1914 almost all of Africa was under European rule; only Ethiopia and Liberia stayed free.
Borders were drawn with little regard for the people living there.

items.name: First World War
facts: The murder of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo set off the war.
Britain, France and Russia fought Germany, Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire.
Trench warfare killed millions; about 9 million soldiers died.
It ended with an armistice on 11 November 1918.

items.name: Russian Revolution
facts: The Tsar was overthrown in March 1917.
In November the Bolsheviks, led by Lenin, seized power.
The world's first communist state, the Soviet Union, was formed in 1922.

items.name: Spanish flu
facts: A flu pandemic killed around 50 million people worldwide.
It killed more people than the First World War.
It was called Spanish flu because Spain's press reported it freely.

items.name: Great Depression
facts: The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 started a world slump.
Banks failed, trade fell and a quarter of American workers lost their jobs.
Hardship helped extreme parties, including Hitler's Nazis, who took power in 1933.

items.name: Second World War
facts: Germany's invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 began the war.
It became the deadliest war in history, killing 70 to 85 million people.
Germany surrendered in May 1945, Japan in August.
Britain, the USA and the Soviet Union were the main Allies.

items.name: The Holocaust
facts: Nazi Germany murdered about six million Jews.
Most were killed in death camps such as Auschwitz or shot in mass killings.
Roma, disabled people and other groups were also murdered.

items.name: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
facts: The USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on 6 August and Nagasaki on 9 August.
Around 110,000 people died at once, and many more later from injuries and radiation.
Japan surrendered on 15 August 1945.

items.name: United Nations founded
facts: Fifty countries signed the UN Charter in San Francisco.
Its aim is to keep peace and help nations work together.
The Security Council has five permanent members: USA, Russia, China, Britain and France.

items.name: Indian independence and partition
facts: Britain left India after a long campaign led by Gandhi and Nehru.
The land was split into India and Pakistan.
Up to 15 million people moved, and hundreds of thousands, perhaps a million, were killed.

items.name: Cold War
facts: The USA and the Soviet Union competed without fighting each other directly.
Both built thousands of nuclear weapons.
NATO formed in 1949 and the Warsaw Pact in 1955.
It ended when the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.

items.name: State of Israel founded
facts: Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948 as British rule in Palestine ended.
Neighbouring Arab states attacked and lost.
About 700,000 Palestinians fled or were driven out; they call this the Nakba.

items.name: Chinese Revolution
facts: Mao Zedong's communists won the civil war against the Nationalists.
The People's Republic of China was declared on 1 October 1949.
The Nationalists fled to Taiwan.
Mao's Great Leap Forward of 1958 to 1962 caused a famine that killed tens of millions.

items.name: Vietnam War
facts: Communist North Vietnam fought the South and its American ally.
The USA sent over 500,000 troops but withdrew in 1973.
Saigon fell in 1975 and Vietnam was united under communist rule.

items.name: US civil rights movement
facts: Black Americans campaigned to end segregation and win equal rights.
Martin Luther King gave his I Have a Dream speech in 1963.
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned segregation.
King was murdered in 1968.

items.name: Decolonisation of Africa
facts: Ghana became the first black African colony to win independence, in 1957.
Seventeen countries became independent in 1960 alone.
Portugal's colonies were among the last, in 1975.

items.name: Cuban Missile Crisis
facts: The USA found Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba.
For 13 days in October the world stood on the edge of nuclear war.
Khrushchev withdrew the missiles; the USA secretly removed its missiles from Turkey.

items.name: Moon landing
facts: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969.
Armstrong said: that's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.
Twelve people walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972.

items.name: Fall of the Berlin Wall
facts: East Germany opened the wall on 9 November 1989.
Communist governments across eastern Europe collapsed that year.
Germany was reunited in 1990.

items.name: World Wide Web
facts: Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist at CERN, invented the Web.
The first website went online in 1991.
The Web runs on the older internet, which dates from the 1960s and 1970s.

items.name: Soviet Union dissolved
facts: The Soviet Union broke up into 15 independent countries on 26 December 1991.
Gorbachev's reforms had loosened control; a failed coup in August sped the collapse.
The Cold War was over.

items.name: End of apartheid
facts: South Africa held its first election open to all races.
Nelson Mandela, freed from prison in 1990, became president.
Apartheid had separated people by race since 1948.

items.name: Rwandan genocide
facts: In about 100 days Hutu extremists killed around 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu.
The world failed to intervene.
The killing ended when Tutsi-led forces took the country.

items.name: 9/11 attacks
facts: Al-Qaeda hijackers flew planes into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon on 11 September 2001.
Nearly 3,000 people died.
The USA and its allies invaded Afghanistan within weeks.

items.name: Iraq War
facts: A US-led coalition, including Britain, invaded Iraq and removed Saddam Hussein.
The claimed weapons of mass destruction were never found.
Years of violence followed.

items.name: Financial crisis
facts: A crash in US housing loans spread through the banks.
Lehman Brothers collapsed in September 2008.
Governments bailed out banks and the world fell into recession.

items.name: Arab Spring
facts: Protests began in Tunisia and spread across the Arab world.
Rulers fell in Tunisia, Egypt and Libya.
Syria fell into a civil war that killed hundreds of thousands.

items.name: Paris climate agreement
facts: Almost every country agreed to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius.
Each country set its own targets for cutting emissions.
Global temperatures have risen by more than 1 degree since 1850.

items.name: Brexit referendum
facts: The UK voted to leave the European Union by 52 to 48 per cent.
Britain had joined in 1973.
It formally left on 31 January 2020.

items.name: Covid-19 pandemic
facts: A new coronavirus spread from Wuhan, China, around the world.
Countries locked down; schools, shops and borders closed.
Around 7 million deaths were recorded; the true figure is probably far higher.
Vaccines were developed within a year.

items.name: Russian invasion of Ukraine
facts: Russia launched a full-scale invasion on 24 February 2022.
Russia had already seized Crimea in 2014.
It became the biggest war in Europe since 1945.
